title: Line Plots with Halves and Quarters

steps.body: A **line plot** stacks an X above a number line for each measurement. When we measure lengths, the line is marked in **halves and quarters** — the very fourths you placed in the fractions course. Each X sits above the value it measured; taller stacks mean that value came up more often.
Build the line plot one measurement at a time.

widget.prompt: Build the pencil-length plot: three pencils are 2 inches, one is 2½ inches, and four are 3 inches.
widget.partialFeedback: Each pencil adds one X above its measured length. Check all three stacks.
widget.successFeedback: The plot has 3 X's at 2, 1 X at 2½, and 4 X's at 3. Every X stands for one pencil.

predict.prompt: On a line plot of pencil lengths, what does each X stand for?
predict.reveal: Every X is one pencil filed above its length — the plot counts THINGS at each value. Stack height tells how many pencils matched, not how long they are.

explanationVariants: The tallest stack of X's marks the most common value — 3 inches, with 4 X's.
Most common = the fullest column: the 3-inch mark leads with four X's.

widget.prompt: In that pencil plot (2 → 3 X's, 2½ → 1 X, 3 → 4 X's), which length is MOST common?

options.label: 3 inches
options.feedback: Its stack of 4 X's is the tallest — the most-measured length.

options.label: 2½ inches
options.feedback: 2½ has just 1 X — the RAREST length here, not the most common.

options.label: 2 inches
options.feedback: 2 inches has 3 X's — close, but the 3-inch stack is taller at 4.

options.label: They're all equal
options.feedback: The stacks differ: 3, 1, and 4 X's. The 3-inch mark wins.

steps.body: The marks between the whole numbers are fractions doing real work. A pencil measured at **2½ inches** lands its X on the halfway mark; one at **2¼** lands a quarter of the way past 2. The line plot is the fraction number line, wearing a lab coat.

explanationVariants: Every X is one measurement, so add all the stacks: 3 + 1 + 4 = 8 pencils.
Count every X across the whole plot: 3 + 1 + 4 = 8.

widget.prompt: In the pencil plot (2 → 3 X's, 2½ → 1 X, 3 → 4 X's), how many pencils were measured in all?

commonErrors.feedback: 3 counted the MARKS (2, 2½, 3) — but each X is a pencil. Add all the X's: 3 + 1 + 4.
4 is the tallest single stack. The total adds EVERY stack: 3 + 1 + 4 = 8.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Every X is one pencil — add all the stacks.

widget.prompt: Four ribbons are measured. Drop each ribbon's X above the right mark on the inch line.

items.label: A ribbon exactly 3½ inches
items.feedback: Three and a half lands its X on the halfway mark between 3 and 4.

items.label: A ribbon exactly 4 inches
items.feedback: A whole 4 inches sits right on the 4 mark.

items.label: A ribbon exactly 3 inches
items.feedback: Three inches even — its X goes above the 3 mark.

items.label: Another ribbon of 3½ inches
items.feedback: Same length as the first — its X stacks above the 3½ mark too.

widget.missFeedback: Each ribbon's X goes above the mark matching its measured length — halves land halfway between wholes.
widget.successFeedback: Two X's stack at 3½, one each at 3 and 4 — the plot is taking shape.

explanationVariants: The shortest measured length is 3 and the longest is 4 — the plot spans from 3 to 4 inches.
Range = from the smallest X-mark to the largest: 3 up to 4.

widget.prompt: That ribbon plot has X's at 3, 3½, and 4 inches. Between which lengths do ALL the ribbons fall?

options.label: Between 3 and 4 inches
options.feedback: The shortest is 3, the longest is 4 — every ribbon lands in that span.

options.label: Between 0 and 4 inches
options.feedback: The range starts at the shortest measurement — the plot's smallest X is at 3, so nothing falls below it.

options.label: Between 3½ and 4 inches
options.feedback: The 3-inch ribbon falls below 3½ — the span must start at the shortest measurement, which is 3.

options.label: They're all exactly 3½
options.feedback: Only some are 3½ — others measure 3 and 4. The lengths spread from 3 to 4.

hints: Only the HALF marks count here — 2½ and 3½, not the whole numbers.
The 2½ mark has 2 X's; the 3½ mark has 3 X's.
Add just those two half-mark stacks.
explanationVariants: The half-inch marks are 2½ (2 X's) and 3½ (3 X's): 2 + 3 = 5 leaves measured at a half-inch.
Ignore the whole-number stacks; total only the half marks: 2 + 3 = 5.

widget.prompt: A leaf plot has X's at: 2 (4 X's), 2½ (2 X's), 3 (1 X), 3½ (3 X's). How many leaves measured a HALF-inch length (ending in ½)?

commonErrors.feedback: 10 added every stack — but the question wants only the HALF marks (2½ and 3½): 2 + 3.
2 took just the 2½ mark. The 3½ mark is also a half-length — add its 3 X's: 2 + 3 = 5.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Add only the stacks above the ½ marks: 2½ and 3½.

takeaways: A line plot stacks one X per measurement above a number line.
The line is marked in halves and quarters — the fraction line at work.
Tallest stack = most common; add all X's for the total; ends give the range.
steps.teaser: next chapter: covering space with squares — the start of area.

concept.body: Quick rewind. A line plot is a **stack of votes above a fraction ruler** — each X is one measurement standing over the exact length it measured. Count the X's in a column to see how many measurements landed on that length.

explanationVariants: Three X's stacked means three measurements landed there.
Each X is one measurement — count them: 3.

widget.prompt: A line plot has 3 X's stacked above the 5-inch mark. How many things measured 5 inches?

options.feedback: Three X's, three measurements at that length.
5 is the LENGTH on the ruler — the X's above it count how many. There are 3.
8 added the mark and the X's (5 + 3). Just count the X's: 3.
